niche.title: The Prisoner Who Demanded a Lawyer — Gideon v. Wainwright | Criminal Law 101
niche.description:
In 1961, a poor drifter named Clarence Earl Gideon was charged with breaking into the Bay Harbor Poolroom in Panama City, Florida — a felony. He couldn't afford a lawyer, and the judge refused to appoint one. From a prison cell, Gideon hand-wrote a five-page petition in pencil and mailed it to the U.S. Supreme Court. On March 18, 1963, the Court ruled 9–0: every state must provide a lawyer to a poor defendant charged with a felony. Betts v. Brady was overruled. Gideon got a retrial — and walked free after one hour.

The case: Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U.S. 335 (1963)
